items.title: Explain how radiation therapy exploits cancer-cell sensitivity
items.reason: Preserve the therapeutic point: radiation can kill cancer cells, and treatment targets the tumor while allowing recovery of normal tissue. Successful treatment does not require every treated cancer to be intrinsically more radiosensitive than surrounding normal cells; dose targeting and treatment timing also contribute. Only the original second sentence is replaced.

Thus, cancer cells are more sensitive to radiation than normal cells and can be killed by it easily. Cancer is characterized by a malfunction of cell reproduction, and can also be caused by ionizing radiation. Without contradiction, ionizing radiation can be both a cure and a cause.</para>

Cancer is characterized by a malfunction of cell reproduction, and can also be caused by ionizing radiation. Without contradiction, ionizing radiation can be both a cure and a cause.</para>

items.title: Distinguish cancer risk from heritable effects
items.reason: The first two sentences imply exactly two established late effects in humans and conflate cellular mutations with inherited effects. Change only the opening; retain the approved FC29 low-dose discussion.
items.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id952989">The two known long-term effects of radiation are cancer and genetic defects. Both are directly attributable to the interference of radiation with cell reproduction. For high doses of radiation, the risk of cancer is reasonably well known from studies of exposed groups. Hiroshima and Nagasaki survivors and a smaller number of people exposed by their occupation, such as radium dial painters, have been fully documented. Chernobyl victims will be studied for many decades, with some data already available. For example, a significant increase in childhood thyroid cancer has been observed. The risk of a radiation-induced cancer for low and moderate doses is generally <emphasis effect="italics">assumed</emphasis> to be proportional to the risk known for high doses. Under this assumption, any dose of radiation, no matter how small, involves a risk to human health. This is called the <term id="import-auto-id1381282">linear hypothesis</term>, or linear no-threshold model, and is used in radiation protection. The size of the cancer risk at very low doses remains uncertain. Cells can repair radiation damage, but some damage may remain or be repaired incorrectly.</para>

items.title: Distinguish charged-particle range from photon attenuation
items.reason: Author-written replacement with limited factual adjustments: restrict the energy/range trend to alpha and beta particles, and clarify that photons have no definite stopping range. Retain the original definition, term ID and figure reference. Photon interaction probabilities need not decrease monotonically with energy.
items.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1229298">The <term id="import-auto-id1587169">range of radiation</term> is defined to be the distance it can travel through a material. Range is related to several factors, including the energy of the radiation, the material encountered, and the type of radiation (see <link target-id="import-auto-id3385282" />). The higher the <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">energy</emphasis></emphasis>, the greater the range, all other factors being the same. This makes good sense, since radiation loses its energy in materials primarily by producing ionization in them, and each ionization of an atom or a molecule requires energy that is removed from the radiation. The amount of ionization is, thus, directly proportional to the energy of the particle of radiation, as is its range.</para>
items.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1229298">The <term id="import-auto-id1587169">range of radiation</term> is defined to be the distance it can travel through a material. Range is related to several factors, including the energy of the radiation, the material encountered, and the type of radiation (see <link target-id="import-auto-id3385282" />). For alpha and beta particles, all other factors being the same, the higher the energy, the greater the range. These particles lose energy through many interactions with the material, so a more energetic particle travels farther before stopping. Gamma ray photons are absorbed or scattered in interactions whose probabilities depend on photon energy and the material; they do not have a definite stopping range.</para>

items.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1927034">Very small currents pass harmlessly and unfelt through the body. This happens to you regularly without your knowledge. The threshold of sensation is only 1 mA and, although unpleasant, shocks are apparently harmless for currents less than 5 mA. A great number of safety rules take the 5-mA value for the maximum allowed shock. At 10 to 20 mA and above, the current can stimulate sustained muscular contractions much as regular nerve impulses do. People sometimes say they were knocked across the room by a shock, but what really happened was that certain muscles contracted, propelling them in a manner not of their own choosing. (See <link target-id="import-auto-id1431810" />(a).) More frightening, and potentially more dangerous, is the “can’t let go” effect illustrated in <link target-id="import-auto-id1431810" />(b). The muscles that close the fingers are stronger than those that open them, so the hand closes involuntarily on the wire shocking it. This can prolong the shock indefinitely. It can also be a danger to a person trying to rescue the victim, because the rescuer’s hand may close about the victim’s wrist. Usually the best way to help the victim is to give the fist a hard knock/blow/jar with an insulator or to throw an insulator at the fist. Modern electric fences, used in animal enclosures, are now pulsed on and off to allow people who touch them to get free, rendering them less lethal than in the past.</para>

items.title: Current path, ECT, and high-frequency heating
items.reason: Keep the frequency and nerve-stimulation discussion. ECT has cardiovascular effects; high-frequency current is not confined to skin. Retain the medical application without presenting it as harmless. Both substitutions are displayed together because they affect the same paragraph.
items.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1926340">Factors other than current that affect the severity of a shock are its path, duration, and AC frequency. Path has obvious consequences. For example, the heart is unaffected by an electric shock through the brain, such as may be used to treat manic depression. And it is a general truth that the longer the duration of a shock, the greater its effects. <link target-id="import-auto-id3190768" /> presents a graph that illustrates the effects of frequency on a shock. The curves show the minimum current for two different effects, as a function of frequency. The lower the current needed, the more sensitive the body is at that frequency. Ironically, the body is most sensitive to frequencies near the 50- or 60-Hz frequencies in common use. The body is slightly less sensitive for DC (<m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>f</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{f=0} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>), mildly confirming Edison’s claims that AC presents a greater hazard. At higher and higher frequencies, the body becomes progressively less sensitive to any effects that involve nerves. This is related to the maximum rates at which nerves can fire or be stimulated. At very high frequencies, electrical current travels only on the surface of a person. Thus a wart can be burned off with very high frequency current without causing the heart to stop. (Do not try this at home with 60-Hz AC!) Some of the spectacular demonstrations of electricity, in which high-voltage arcs are passed through the air and over people’s bodies, employ high frequencies and low currents. (See <link target-id="import-auto-id3163065" />.) </para>

items.title: Microshock requires a path to the heart
items.reason: Do not imply every IV or break in skin creates the same sensitivity as an intracardiac connection. Remove the unsupported 20-microamp surgical assertion and fixed 1/1000 multiplier. Keep microampere versus milliampere scale and the term anchor.

items.title: Compact modern treatment of radiation dose
items.reason: Option 1 selected: distinguish absorbed dose, equivalent dose, and effective dose; replace the conflation of RBE and quality factor with standardized radiation weighting, retaining the simple alpha/gamma calculation and rad/rem conversions.
items.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id2681649">The effects of ionizing radiation may be directly proportional to the dose in rads, but they also depend on the type of radiation and the type of tissue. That is, for a given dose in rads, the effects depend on whether the radiation is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi fontstyle="italic">α,</m:mi><m:mspace width="0.25em" /><m:mi fontstyle="italic">β,</m:mi><m:mspace width="0.25em" /><m:mi fontstyle="italic">γ,</m:mi></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{α,`β`,γ,} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> X-ray, or some other type of ionizing radiation. In the earlier discussion of the range of ionizing radiation, it was noted that energy is deposited in a series of ionizations and not in a single interaction. Each ion pair or ionization requires a certain amount of energy, so that the number of ion pairs is directly proportional to the amount of the deposited ionizing energy. But, if the range of the radiation is small, as it is for <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>α</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{α} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> s, then the ionization and the damage created is more concentrated and harder for the organism to repair, as seen in <link target-id="import-auto-id1860748" />. Concentrated damage is more difficult for biological organisms to repair than damage that is spread out, so short-range particles have greater biological effects. The <term id="import-auto-id1840138">relative biological effectiveness</term> (RBE) or <term id="import-auto-id3104618">quality factor</term><emphasis effect="bold" /> (QF)<sup /> is given in <link target-id="import-auto-id3172969" /> for several types of ionizing radiation—the effect of the radiation is directly proportional to the RBE. A dose unit more closely related to effects in biological tissue is called the <term id="import-auto-id3090228">roentgen equivalent man</term> or rem and is defined to be the dose in rads multiplied by the relative biological effectiveness.</para>
items.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id2681649">The effects of ionizing radiation depend on the absorbed dose, the type of radiation, and the type of tissue. For a given absorbed dose, densely concentrated ionization, such as that produced by α particles, can cause damage that is harder to repair (see <link target-id="import-auto-id1860748"/>). The <term id="import-auto-id1840138">relative biological effectiveness</term> (RBE) compares the absorbed doses of a reference radiation and the radiation being studied that produce the same biological effect. It depends on the effect being measured. For radiation protection, standardized <emphasis effect="bold">radiation weighting factors</emphasis>, <m:math><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>w</m:mi><m:mi>R</m:mi></m:msub></m:mrow></m:math>, are used instead (see <link target-id="import-auto-id3172969"/>). For one type of radiation, the <emphasis effect="bold">equivalent dose</emphasis> H to an organ or tissue is its average absorbed dose D multiplied by the radiation weighting factor. Absorbed dose is measured in grays (Gy); equivalent dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). The related <term id="import-auto-id3104618">quality factor</term> is used in dose-equivalent quantities for radiation monitoring; it is not another name for RBE. (c) Alphas have the smallest range, betas have a greater range, and gammas penetrate the farthest.</caption>

(b) Charged particles generally lose energy over shorter distances in materials with higher electron density. (c) The illustration shows the usual penetration pattern for radioactive emissions: alphas stop over short distances, betas penetrate farther, and gammas are more penetrating.</caption>

context_passages.title: Approved F2-06: earlier range explanation
context_passages.xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1229298">The <term id="import-auto-id1587169">range of radiation</term> is defined to be the distance it can travel through a material. Range is related to several factors, including the energy of the radiation, the material encountered, and the type of radiation (see <link target-id="import-auto-id3385282" />). For alpha and beta particles, all other factors being the same, the higher the energy, the greater the range. These particles lose energy through many interactions with the material, so a more energetic particle travels farther before stopping. Gamma ray photons are absorbed or scattered in interactions whose probabilities depend on photon energy and the material; they do not have a definite stopping range.</para>

context_passages.xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id3253816">Alpha radiation from radioactive sources has a range much less than a millimeter of biological tissues, usually not enough to even penetrate the dead layers of our skin. On the other hand, the same <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>α</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> radiation can penetrate a few centimeters of air, so mere distance from a source prevents <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>α</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{α} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> radiation from reaching us. This makes <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>α</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{α} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> radiation less penetrating from outside the body than <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>β</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>γ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{γ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> radiation. If alpha-emitting material enters the body, it can severely damage nearby tissue. Typical <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mi>β</m:mi></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> radiation can penetrate a few millimeters of tissue or about a meter of air. Beta radiation is thus hazardous even when not ingested. Beta particles can be stopped by shielding, but their slowing can produce bremsstrahlung X-rays, particularly in materials such as lead. Plastic is often used to stop beta particles while limiting this X-ray production; additional shielding may be needed for the X-rays. Gamma rays do not have a well-defined stopping range, but they are effectively shielded—that is, reduced in intensity to acceptable levels—by sufficient shielding, often many centimeters of lead. The required thickness depends on the photon energy, source strength, and exposure conditions. One benefit of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>γ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{γ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>s is that they allow radioactive tracers to be detected (see <link target-id="import-auto-id2589483" />).</para>
